passage: I'm Kashish, and I sit next to Shreya. Today two boys kept talking during the test, so Ma'am said the whole class would lose recess. Everyone groaned. Shreya put her hand up. Her voice shook a bit, but she said, "Ma'am, is it fair to punish everyone for what two people did?" The room went silent. Ma'am thought for a moment. "Maybe not. The two talkers will stay in. The rest can go." I wasn't sure if Shreya was scared or just brave. Maybe both.

qa.q: Why did Ma'am say the whole class would lose recess?
qa.a: Because two boys kept talking during the test.

qa.q: What does Shreya's shaking voice suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous about speaking up to the teacher.

qa.q: What could students learn from how Shreya raised her concern?
qa.a: They can question a rule politely with a clear reason instead of complaining.

qa.q: How might Ma'am see Shreya's question?
qa.a: She seems to take it seriously and agree the punishment was unfair to the rest.

grounding: A classmate observes a child questioning whether a group punishment is fair.

passage:
Week one: The school's new rule said anyone late to assembly would miss games period. On Monday the bus broke down and Minakshi missed games. "It wasn't my fault!" she told Rafiq, her father, at dinner. "Is it fair?" he asked. "Not for bus kids."
Week two: Minakshi and three others wrote a letter to the principal explaining that late buses weren't their choice. Rafiq helped with spelling but not ideas.
Week three: The principal changed the rule: bus delays wouldn't count. Minakshi ran to games period grinning.

qa.q: What broke down on Monday?
qa.a: The bus broke down.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's "It wasn't my fault!" show about her feelings?
qa.a: It shows she felt the punishment was unfair and frustrating.

qa.q: What went right in how Minakshi challenged the rule?
qa.a: She and others wrote a clear, polite letter explaining why the rule was unfair to bus children.

qa.q: How might other bus children be affected by the rule change?
qa.a: They won't be punished for delays they can't control, which feels fairer.

grounding: It shows a child judging a rule's fairness and working to make it proportionate over weeks.

passage: "Zainab, you think your team's rule is unfair? Let me tell you about my hockey days. Our coach once benched the whole team for a match because one girl came late. We lost badly. Afterwards I asked him, 'Should eleven people pay for one person's mistake?' He was quiet. The next season he made new rules: the late person runs extra laps, not the whole team. Nobody complained. Fairness means the consequence fits the mistake and the person." Aditi Phuphi sipped her tea. "Now, what's happening in your team?"

qa.q: Why did Aditi's coach bench the whole team?
qa.a: Because one girl came late.

qa.q: What might Aditi have been feeling when she asked the coach her question?
qa.a: She likely felt the punishment was unfair and was frustrated by losing.

qa.q: What lesson does Aditi share about fair consequences?
qa.a: That a consequence should fit the mistake and fall on the person who made it.

qa.q: How might the late girl have felt about the whole team being benched?
qa.a: She probably felt guilty that everyone paid for her mistake.

grounding: An elder tells a story of debating whether a team punishment was proportionate and fair.

passage: The school bus left in ten minutes, and class six was still sitting in silence. Someone had drawn a moustache on the principal's photo, and nobody owned up, so Mrs Rao had cancelled sports day practice for all of them. Siddharth, eleven, raised his hand. 'Ma'am, can I say something quickly?' She nodded. 'The drawing was wrong. But forty kids losing practice for one person's joke feels too big. And some of us weren't even in the room.' Pradeep whispered, 'You'll get us in more trouble.' Mrs Rao tapped her pen. 'What would be fair, then?' 'Only those who were here stay back and clean it. Everyone else practises.' She thought, then agreed.

qa.q: Why had Mrs Rao cancelled sports day practice?
qa.a: Someone drew a moustache on the principal's photo and nobody owned up.

qa.q: What was Pradeep worried about when Siddharth spoke up?
qa.a: Pradeep feared that questioning the teacher would make things worse for the whole class.

qa.q: What made Siddharth's argument persuasive?
qa.a: He admitted the drawing was wrong, explained why the punishment was too big, and offered a fairer alternative.

qa.q: How might the children who weren't in the room see the new decision?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and that they had been treated fairly at last.

grounding: Shows a child debating whether a group punishment is proportionate and fair to all, under time pressure.

passage: In their Jaipur colony, the cricket rule was clear: hit the ball into Mrs Kulkarni's garden and you were banned for a week. On Sunday, Anand, nine, swung hard and the ball sailed over her hedge. He knew the rule, but his stomach dropped. 'A whole week? It was an accident!' Disha, his twelve-year-old sister, was captain. 'Rules are rules.' 'But when Bunty hit it there on purpose last month, he also got one week. That's the same for doing it on purpose and by mistake.' Disha frowned. Other kids gathered. 'Okay,' she said slowly, 'so maybe first accident is just out. On purpose, one week.' Everyone voted. Anand fetched the ball and said sorry to Mrs Kulkarni.

qa.q: What was the colony rule about Mrs Kulkarni's garden?
qa.a: Anyone who hit the ball into her garden was banned for a week.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when the ball went over the hedge?
qa.a: He felt a sinking dread, since he knew the rule, and then it seemed unfair because it was an accident.

qa.q: What made Anand's point about Bunty a strong one?
qa.a: He showed the same punishment was given for an accident and a deliberate act, which isn't proportionate.

qa.q: Why might Disha have changed her mind as captain?
qa.a: She saw that treating an accident like a deliberate hit wasn't fair to everyone, and a vote kept the group together.

grounding: Shows children debating whether a punishment is proportionate and revising a rule fairly.

passage:
“A week without the phone? Just because I was ten minutes late?” Vaibhav, nine, slammed his bag down.
His brother Harsha, twelve, looked up from his homework. “What was the rule?”
“Home by six. I was ten past.”
“And the punishment for being late?”
“Mummy never said. She just decided.”
Harsha thought. “Ten minutes and a whole week does seem big. But you didn't call.”
Vaibhav went quiet. “My battery died.”
“Then tell her that. Ask if a day is fairer, and say you'll call next time.”
Vaibhav took a breath. “Will you come with me?”
“Okay. But you do the talking.”

qa.q: What time was Vaibhav supposed to be home?
qa.a: Home by six.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel about losing the phone for a week?
qa.a: He felt angry and that it was unfair, slamming his bag.

qa.q: What did Harsha suggest to make it fairer?
qa.a: To explain the dead battery, ask if a day is fairer and promise to call next time.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Vaibhav's request?
qa.a: She may appreciate him explaining calmly and be willing to change the punishment.

grounding: Two brothers debate whether a punishment fits a small rule-break.

passage:
In Class 5, Kiran-ma'am had a rule: if anyone talked during silent reading, the whole class lost PE.
One Friday, one boy talked. We all lost PE. I'm Vaibhav, and I remember feeling it wasn't fair. I hadn't said a word.
At home, I thought about it. Punishing everyone made the others angry at that boy, not at the talking.
On Monday I asked Kiran-ma'am if I could say something. I said, “Maybe only the person who talks should lose PE, and the rest of us shouldn't.” My voice shook.
She thought, then asked the class to vote on a new rule. We did.

qa.q: What was the class rule about talking during silent reading?
qa.a: If anyone talked, the whole class lost PE.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel about losing PE?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt it was unfair and a bit angry, having not said a word.

qa.q: Why was Vaibhav's suggestion fairer?
qa.a: It only punished the person who broke the rule, not everyone.

qa.q: How did Kiran-ma'am respond to Vaibhav?
qa.a: She listened, thought and asked the class to vote on a new rule.

grounding: A student questions whether a group punishment is fair and suggests a better rule.

passage:
Student council note. Teacher adviser: Manoj Deshmukh.
This week the council discussed a case: a Class 6 boy broke a window while playing cricket at break. Some members wanted him suspended for a week.
Vikas (twelve) disagreed. He said suspension was too big for an accident, and wouldn't fix the window. He suggested the boy help the caretaker repair it and write an apology.
Others argued that rules need strong punishments. Vikas listened, then asked, “Does the punishment fit what happened?”
The council voted for Vikas's idea. The headmistress agreed.
Next step: I've asked Vikas to help draft a fairer list of consequences.

qa.q: What did some council members want for the boy?
qa.a: They wanted him suspended for a week.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel about the suspension idea?
qa.a: He felt uneasy that it was unfair and too big for an accident.

qa.q: What did Vikas suggest, and why was it fairer?
qa.a: Helping the caretaker repair the window and writing an apology, because it matched the accident and fixed the harm.

qa.q: How might the boy who broke the window feel about the council's decision?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and more willing to put things right.

grounding: A teacher notes a twelve-year-old arguing that a punishment should fit the mistake.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was SO unfair. Siddharth and two others were talking during the maths test, and Ms Iyer cancelled PE for the WHOLE class. I didn't say a word!
At lunch I told Siddharth, "It's your fault." He said, "It's her rule. I didn't cancel PE."
I kept thinking. Punishing everyone makes us angry at the talkers, not at the talking. And the quiet ones get punished for nothing.
So after lunch I asked Ms Iyer, politely, if only the talkers could miss PE. She listened. She said she'd think about it, and that maybe next time she'd give a warning first.
I'm still annoyed. But I'm glad I asked.
— Saurabh

qa.q: Who cancelled PE for the whole class?
qa.a: Ms Iyer.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling about the PE decision?
qa.a: Saurabh felt angry and wronged, because he was punished though he hadn't talked.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that others in the class could copy?
qa.a: He thought about why the rule felt unfair and then politely raised it with the teacher.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the punishment?
qa.a: Siddharth sees it as the teacher's rule, not his fault, and doesn't take the blame.

grounding: In his diary a child questions whether a whole-class punishment is fair and raises it politely.

passage:
On the village cricket ground, the rule was: whoever hits the ball into Maria aunty's garden is out and must fetch it.
Vishal hit a huge six that sailed into the garden. "Out!" everyone shouted.
Maria, Maria aunty's niece, who was playing too, said, "Wait. Why should a big hit be out? He hit it well."
"Because Aunty shouts."
"Then the rule should be: fetch it and say sorry, but not out."
The boys argued. Vishal said, "Only fair if it's the same for everybody."
They agreed. Vishal fetched the ball, said sorry to Maria aunty, and kept batting.

qa.q: Whose garden did the ball go into?
qa.a: Maria aunty's garden.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when everyone shouted "Out!"?
qa.a: Vishal felt frustrated and cheated, since his best shot got him out.

qa.q: Which part of the children's new rule made it fairer?
qa.a: They talked about why the rule existed and made a new one that fixed the real problem and applied to everyone.

qa.q: How might Maria aunty see the new rule?
qa.a: Maria aunty would probably be happier getting an apology each time, instead of just angry shouting.

grounding: Village children debate whether a cricket rule's punishment is fair and change it.

passage:
At the school in Santiago, the rule was: late homework gets zero, no matter what.
Camila had been sick with fever all weekend and handed in her project on Tuesday. Zero.
Hiroshi, who sat next to her, frowned. "That's not fair. She wasn't lazy. She was sick."
"Rules are rules," said another boy.
"But the rule is to stop lazy people, not sick ones," Hiroshi said.
At the class meeting, Hiroshi and Camila suggested: late for a good reason, bring a note, no zero. The teacher listened, and the class voted. The rule changed.
Camila's project got its mark.

qa.q: What did the rule say about late homework?
qa.a: Late homework gets zero, no matter what.

qa.q: What was Hiroshi feeling when he frowned?
qa.a: Hiroshi felt it was unfair and was upset for Camila.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi and Camila do that made the change possible?
qa.a: They explained the rule's purpose and suggested a fair exception at the class meeting, instead of just complaining.

qa.q: What is it like for Camila when her project finally gets its mark?
qa.a: Camila likely feels relieved and respected, knowing her illness was taken into account.

grounding: Children in Chile question a rigid homework rule and propose a fairer one.

passage:
In the hostel study hall, the warden announced that because two boys had been talking after lights-out, the whole of Dorm C would lose television on Saturday.
Raghav raised his hand. "Sir, can I ask something? Twenty of us were asleep."
"Rules are rules," the warden said.
Gurpreet stood up too, carefully polite. "We're not saying no punishment, Sir. Just that it lands on the ones who did it. Otherwise next time nobody will bother keeping quiet, because we'll lose it anyway."
The warden rubbed his forehead. "And what would you suggest?"
They thought about it. Raghav said the two boys could lose television and help sweep the dorm, and everyone else keeps it. The warden said he'd think about it. On Saturday, eighteen boys watched the match, and two swept.

qa.q: What did the warden say Dorm C would lose on Saturday?
qa.a: The warden said the whole of Dorm C would lose television on Saturday.

qa.q: How can you tell Gurpreet was nervous about challenging the warden?
qa.a: Gurpreet stood up "carefully polite" and began by saying they weren't against punishment, which suggests Gurpreet felt anxious not to seem rude.

qa.q: Which choice made the warden listen, and why?
qa.a: Suggesting a fairer punishment instead of just complaining worked, because it showed the boys wanted rules kept, not avoided.

qa.q: How might the two boys who talked see the new decision?
qa.a: They might feel a bit ashamed but also treated fairly, because the punishment fit what they did and the others didn't resent them.

grounding: Illustrates children debating, respectfully and with a proposal, whether a group punishment is fair.

passage:
Summer holidays, and my little brother Raghav became our building's lawyer. I'm Rekha, and I watched the whole thing from the stairs.
During the evening cricket, Monty from 3B hit a ball through the watchman's window. The big boys decided he was banned from playing for the whole summer. Monty went red and sat on the steps.
Raghav marched up. "Whole summer is too much. It was an accident. Last year Chintu broke a light and got one week."
"So what, he just gets away with it?" someone said.
"No. He says sorry to Bhaskar Uncle and helps clear the glass, and he's out for a week." Raghav's voice wobbled, but he didn't back off.
They argued for ten minutes. In the end, one week. I don't know if Raghav was scared. He looked it.

qa.q: How long did the big boys first ban Monty from playing?
qa.a: They first banned Monty from playing for the whole summer.

qa.q: What does Raghav's wobbling voice suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Raghav was probably nervous and a bit scared of the bigger boys, but determined enough not to back off.

qa.q: What made Raghav's argument fair rather than just taking Monty's side?
qa.a: He compared it with the one-week ban for Chintu and still asked Monty to apologise and help, so the rule stayed and only the size changed.

qa.q: If you were Monty sitting on the steps, what would you want?
qa.a: You would want someone to see that it was an accident and that a whole summer was too much, while still letting you make it right.

grounding: Shows a child, seen by an older sibling, arguing that a punishment should be proportionate and consistent with past cases.

passage:
Tuesday, cold December morning. Lavanya's project was one day late because the power had gone in her lane all evening. Class rule: late means zero. Ma'am wrote the zero. Jasleen whispered, "That's not fair," and Lavanya stared at her desk, blinking hard.
Thursday. At class council, Lavanya raised it. Her hands were shaking. "The rule's the same for everyone, but the reasons aren't. Someone who forgot and someone with no light both get zero."
Jasleen added, "Maybe a note from home could count?"
Some said it would be misused. They argued it out.
The next Monday, Ma'am brought a new rule: late work loses a little, a real reason with a note loses nothing, and the council could vote on unclear cases. Lavanya got her project marked.

qa.q: Why was Lavanya's project one day late?
qa.a: The power had gone in her lane all evening.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when Ma'am wrote the zero?
qa.a: Lavanya felt upset and wronged, which shows in her staring at her desk and blinking hard.

qa.q: What would you advise a classmate who worries a new rule could be misused?
qa.a: Suggest a safeguard, like needing a note from home and letting the council vote on unclear cases, instead of dropping fairness altogether.

qa.q: How might Ma'am see the change after the council discussion?
qa.a: Ma'am may feel the class has shown it can think about fairness sensibly, and see a rule that fits different reasons as easier to defend.

grounding: Illustrates a child debating over several days whether a single fixed punishment is proportionate and fair to everyone.

passage:
Deepika, you're upset that the whole class lost games period because one boy broke the window. Let me tell you about the Holi when I was ten.
Our teacher found colour thrown on the notice board. Nobody owned up. So she said all forty of us would clean the school for a week. I was furious. I hadn't even brought colour!
My friend Kamla said, "It's fair. Everyone should share."
I said, "Fair means the punishment fits the person who did it."
We argued all the way home. Then we went together to the teacher and asked if the ones who didn't do it could help find a better way. She listened. The boy who did it came forward the next day.
So, beta, what do you think would be fair this time?

qa.q: How many students were told to clean the school for a week?
qa.a: All forty of them.

qa.q: What was the young storyteller feeling when the whole class was punished?
qa.a: The storyteller felt angry and wronged, because they hadn't even brought colour.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed the outcome?
qa.a: Going together to the teacher to ask for a fairer way, instead of just complaining, led her to listen and the real culprit to come forward.

qa.q: How did Kamla see the class punishment differently?
qa.a: Kamla thought it was fair for everyone to share the consequence, so she saw fairness as equal treatment rather than fitting the person.

grounding: Shows an elder helping a child think about whether a group punishment is proportionate and fair.
